data.title: 8 Investor Dos and Don’ts as the STI Heads South
data.description:
It’s official.

The Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) is in a correction.

Last Friday (6 November 2026), the index closed at 5,180, almost 11 per cent below its record close of 5,802 in early September 2026.

Just two months ago, the STI was setting records. 

Today, the mood has turned.

If you feel uneasy, you are not alone. 

In times like these, it’s easy to lose sight of what matters and what doesn’t.

With that in mind, here are eight dos and don’ts for my fellow investors.

1. Do know the odds of a correction …

A fall of 10 per cent or more is not unusual. 

It is the norm.

Historically, the STI has fallen by 10 per cent or more in around eight out of every 10 years.

Source: S&P Global Market Intelligence, Yahoo Finance, WSJ, author’s calculation

Said another way, a year without a correction is the exception, not the rule.

Knowing the odds won’t make a fall painless. 

But it should make it less of a surprise.

2. … but don’t mistake odds for timing

Here’s the catch: knowing a market correction will occur tells you nothing about when it will happen.

Legendary fund manager Peter Lynch once observed that far more money has been lost by investors preparing for corrections than in the corrections themselves.

Imagine you sold your shares when the STI hit a record high of around 3,900 on 10 February 2025 — its first in 17 years — convinced that a fall was overdue.

You would still be behind today. 

Even after an 11 per cent drop, the index is still well above 3,900 — and that’s before counting dividends.

There’s a deeper emotional flaw to consider. 

If fear of a 10 per cent drop makes you sell, that same fear will make it hard to buy back when the drop arrives.

More often than not, the investor who sells early ends up waiting for a lower price — and never acts on it.

3. Do keep an even keel …

Investing in a falling market is not just about which shares to buy, or at what price.

You may land a great bargain. 

But if you lack the stomach to hold, you will be prone to selling at the wrong time.

As Lynch put it, it’s not brains that will help you beat the stock market, it’s your stomach.

Start with the basics. 

Keep cash for emergencies. 

Only invest money you won’t need for the next five years.

If daily price swings are costing you sleep, consider paring back to a level where you feel comfortable.

Here’s a thought: when investing, don’t optimise for performance. Optimise for a calm mind.

A calm mind makes better decisions. 

And better decisions lead to better performance. 

4. … but don’t beat yourself up for not selling

Looking back, September 2026’s peak seems obvious. 

It wasn’t at the time.

Nobel laureate Daniel Kahneman called this hindsight bias: once we know how events unfolded, we convince ourselves we saw it coming.

Documenting your investment moves will help. 

As humans, we tend to misremember our past experiences, especially when they involve major events.   

On this note, the past six years have been full of challenging episodes that can distort our memories and directly impact the lessons we learn.

Therein lies the issue. 

If you remember the wrong things, you will draw the wrong conclusions.

Even worse, you will be applying these wrong lessons in the future over and over again. 

5. Don’t watch the scoreboard …

Warren Buffett once said that games are won by players who focus on the playing field, not by those whose eyes are glued to the scoreboard.

In a correction, the scoreboard — in this case, falling stock prices — is hard to ignore. 

Every red number feels like a verdict on your investments.

But a falling share price only tells you how other investors feel. 

It says little about how the business is doing.

Here’s a simple fix: remove the daily price-change column from your portfolio tracker.

6. … but do watch the business

A share price is made of two things: the business, and the mood of the market.

In a correction, the market’s mood does all the moving. 

Prices swing on headlines and fear.

In contrast, business developments move at a slower pace. 

They show up in what a company actually earns, quarter after quarter, year after year.

Lynch saw the same pattern. 

Measured in months, he said, there is little link between a company’s results and its share price. 

Measured over many years, the link is close to perfect.

So when the results come in, ask one question: is the business still growing?

One quarter shouldn’t change your mind. 

A trend over several quarters might.

If the business keeps growing, a lower share price is not a threat. 

It may well be a gift.

7. Do have a shopping list …

A correction is a good time to list the businesses you want to own for years, not months.

Keep in mind: you should buy because you want to own the business, not because the share price is lower.

Then decide how you will put your money to work. 

Here’s a rule of thumb: take at least half as long to invest your money as it took you to save it.

If you took four years to save S$10,000, there is nothing wrong with taking two years to invest it.

8. … but don’t wait for the perfect price

In March 2020, Citibank’s research team downgraded DBS Group (SGX: D05) to “sell”, saying the shares were worth just S$17.50 — or S$15.90 after adjusting for DBS’s 2024 bonus issue.

I bought shares at S$18.40, above Citi’s target.

Today, DBS trades at just under S$70. My shares are up about 280 per cent, before dividends.

The lesson? You don’t need to get the perfect price.

Waiting for a “cheap” price comes with a catch. 

Over the past 20 years, DBS has traded at one times book value only three times: during the Global Financial Crisis in 2008, the oil price crash in 2014, and the pandemic in 2020.

Each time, something had to go badly wrong first.

Get Smart: The opportunity you only see in hindsight

After almost two decades of investing, here’s what I’ve learnt: every past market decline looks like an opportunity. 

Every future decline looks like a risk.

Looking back, buying DBS at S$18.40 in March 2020 seems like an easy call. 

It wasn’t. 

Four months later, the Monetary Authority of Singapore asked the local banks to cap their dividends at 60 per cent of the previous year’s level. 

Vaccines were still just a hope.

Today’s correction will likely be no different. 

A few years from now, it may look like an obvious opportunity. 

Right now, it feels like a risk.

That’s why the dos and don’ts matter. 

Know the odds, keep your calm, watch the business, and buy what you want to own, a little at a time.

As Charlie Munger, Buffett’s long-time business partner, said, the big money is not in the buying or selling, but in the waiting.

data.title: What is a Dividend? A Beginner’s Guide to Passive Income in Singapore
data.description:
Ever wondered how you can earn extra income without working extra hours?

Taking your first step into investing can feel overwhelming, but building passive income is simpler than you think. 

Dividend investing lets you become a co-owner in successful companies that share their cash profits directly with you.

Over the next four weeks, The Smart Investor is breaking down everything you need to know.

Whether you are new to investing or preparing for a secure retirement, we are here to help you take those first confident steps toward long-term wealth.

What Is a Dividend and How Does It Work?

A dividend is a payment that a company makes to its shareholders, usually from its profits. 

In Singapore, investors can earn dividend income by owning shares in dividend-paying companies listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX). 

Take the familiar heartland supermarket operator Sheng Siong Group (SGX: OV8) as an example. 

Suppose you purchased 1,000 shares of the company.

In the financial year ended 31 December 2026 (FY2026), Sheng Siong paid a dividend of S$0.07 per share.

That means, as a shareholder, you would have received S$70 in dividends.

But that is not all.

There are two ways to earn money when you buy shares:

  1. Dividends: Cash received from owning shares.
  2. Capital gains: Profit earned when shares are sold at a higher price than their purchase price. 

But it is important to remember that dividends are not guaranteed, and share prices can also rise or fall regardless of dividend payments. 

Why Do Companies Pay Dividends?

When a company turns a profit, there are a few things they can do with that cash.

One, they can reinvest in the business to support future growth.

Two, they can use these earnings to pay down debt.

Established companies with stable businesses often generate predictable cash flow, frequently more than they need to reinvest. 

These companies may choose the third option: pay regular dividends to return that surplus to shareholders. 

This can signal the company’s financial strength and boost shareholders’ confidence in future earnings. 

Familiar names such as DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), Singapore Telecommunications Limited (SGX: Z74), or Singtel, and Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68) are examples of established companies with regular dividend payouts.

However, not all companies pay dividends and paying dividends does not automatically make a company a good investment.

How Much Passive Income Can You Get From Dividends?

A good place to start is the dividend yield, which is calculated as the annual dividend per share divided by the share price, expressed as a percentage.

If you invested S$10,000 in a stock with an annual dividend yield of 3%, that will translate to S$300 a year in dividends.

As illustrated below, a higher yield means more dividend income for the same amount invested. 

Illustrative Dividend Yield Annual Dividend Income
3% S$300
5% S$500
7% S$700

Dividends may be paid quarterly, half-yearly or annually, depending on the company.

However, unlike a monthly salary, dividend income is neither fixed nor guaranteed. 

Where Can Singapore Investors Find Dividend-Paying Stocks?

Investors can buy shares in Singapore-listed companies on SGX.

Two common categories of dividend-paying investments are:

  • Blue-chip stocks: Companies with  long operating histories, strong reputations and consistent financial performance that tend to pay regular dividends, such as DBS and Singtel.
  • Real estate investment trusts (REITs): Trusts that own income-generating properties, collect rent from tenants and distribute rental income to unitholders. For example, Frasers Centrepoint Trust (SGX: J69U) is a leading Singapore suburban retail REIT that owns major heartland malls, including Causeway Point in Woodlands and NEX in Serangoon.

What Can You Do With the Dividends You Receive?

When you receive dividends, you can cash them out and use the income to cover everyday expenses or supplement your retirement income.

Another approach is to reinvest them to buy more shares.

Take the example of 1,000 Sheng Siong shares bought at S$2.36 per share on 3 November 2026.

The table below shows how reinvesting dividends sparks compounding: your new shares start earning their own dividends alongside your original ones. 

Compounding 1,000 Sheng Siong Shares Over Time

Time Horizon Shares Owned Annual Dividends Received (S$) Total Portfolio Value (S$) Total Return (% Gain)
Start (Year 0) 1,000.00 S$70.80 (baseline) S$2,360.00 —
1 Year 1,030.00 S$72.92 S$2,430.80 +3.0%
5 Years 1,159.27 S$82.08 S$2,735.88 +15.9%
10 Years 1,343.92 S$95.15 S$3,171.65 +34.4%
15 Years 1,557.97 S$110.30 S$3,676.81 +55.8%

Note: For illustration only. Assumes a constant 3% yield, constant share price, and full dividend reinvestment.

Over time, this snowball effect steadily expands your position and passive income without costing an extra cent.

What Are the Risks of Dividend Investing?

No investment is 100% risk-free. 

There are three important risks to consider in dividend investing.

First, dividends can be reduced or stopped, as companies may cut payouts when business conditions deteriorate. 

Second, share prices can also fall, and receiving dividends does not prevent investors from losing money on their investments. 

Finally, high yields may look attractive but they can also be red flags in a business. 

It may signal that a company is paying out more than it can afford – or that its stock price has tumbled due to underlying business troubles, pushing its yield up.

Before you invest, take the time to understand the business behind the dividend: how it makes money, whether its earnings are stable and whether it generates enough cash to keep paying shareholders. 

Rather than putting all your eggs in one basket, diversify your holdings across different business sectors and geographic markets to protect and grow your capital.

Get Smart: Your First Step to Passive Income

Think of dividend investing as putting your money to work so you don’t have to work forever.

Dividends let you collect regular passive income from companies you co-own without selling a single share. 

Building lasting wealth takes patience and a focus on solid Singapore businesses, not chasing sky-high yields. 

Start small; there is no need to invest all your savings at one go.

Consider familiar names first, ease in at your own pace, and always align every investment with your personal financial goals.

Now that you know how dividends work, where should you invest?

data.title: S$10,000 in DBS Shares: How Much Dividend Income Could You Receive in 2027?
data.description:
DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05) has long been a local favourite among Singapore investors seeking reliable dividend income.

The group’s popularity stems from its strong banking franchise, consistent profitability and track record of rewarding shareholders.

However, if you had S$10,000 to invest today, how much dividend income could DBS realistically generate in 2027?

In this article, we will examine the numbers and whether the bank’s current valuation makes it an attractive income investment.

How Many DBS Shares Can S$10,000 Buy?

On 6 November 2026, DBS shares closed at S$69.72.

With S$10,000, investors could purchase 140 shares.

This amounts to 14 board lots of 10 shares each, following Singapore Exchange’s reduction of DBS’s board lot size in October 2026.

At this price, the investment would cost S$9,760.80 before brokerage fees.

Assuming a S$10 brokerage fee, investors would have S$229.20 remaining.

Importantly, a higher share price means fewer shares for the same investment.

Had shares been bought at a lower price, the yield on cost would be higher, assuming dividends remain unchanged.

How Much Dividend Income Could DBS Pay in 2027?

DBS has progressively increased its ordinary dividends.

Recently, the bank declared S$0.66 per share for each quarter from 1Q2026 to 3Q2026.

Annualising these quarterly payments gives an ordinary dividend of S$2.64 per share.

Separately, DBS introduced a Capital Return dividend of S$0.15 per share quarterly in 2025, which management plans to maintain through 2027.

This represents another S$0.60 per share annually, although these additional dividends should not be treated as permanent recurring dividends beyond the announced period.

Assuming investors hold 140 DBS shares throughout 2027 and receive four quarterly payments, here are three potential scenarios.

Scenario Ordinary DPS Total 2027 Income*
Conservative S$2.40 S$420
Base Case S$2.64 S$453.60
Optimistic S$2.88 S$487.20

*Includes the S$0.60 annual Capital Return dividend.

Under the base case, investors would receive S$369.60 in ordinary dividends and S$84 in Capital Return dividends, bringing total annual income to S$453.60.

This annual income works out to a monthly equivalent of approximately S$37.80.

The conservative scenario assumes ordinary dividends decline amid weaker earnings.

Meanwhile, the optimistic scenario assumes a further increase supported by stronger profitability.

Can DBS Sustain Its Dividend Payments?

DBS’s latest quarterly results showed some pressure, but overall earnings were resilient.

In the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026), total income fell 1% year on year (YoY) to S$5.85 billion, while net profit declined 5% to S$2.81 billion.

The picture was slightly better when looking at the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), with net profit rising 2% YoY to S$8.82 billion.

For 9M2026, net interest income slipped 1% YoY to S$10.79 billion as lower Singapore interest rates were largely offset by loan growth and hedging.

In 3Q2026 alone, net interest income rose 4% YoY.

Meanwhile, its wealth management business continued to grow strongly.

For 9M2026, wealth management fees grew 24% YoY to S$2.69 billion, contributing to a 15% YoY increase in net fee income to S$4.37 billion.

In addition, DBS reported a Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital ratio of 15.9% as at 20 September 2026.

With annualised earnings per share of S$4.15 for 9M2026 and an annualised ordinary dividend of S$2.64, DBS’s payout ratio works out to approximately 63.6%.

This provides some comfort for income investors, as loan growth and asset quality remained healthy in 9M2026.

However, lower interest rates, slower loan growth or higher credit costs could still put pressure on future earnings.

Is DBS Still Worth Buying for Dividend Income?

At S$69.72 per share, DBS’s annualised ordinary dividend of S$2.64 gives a yield of approximately 3.8%.

The inclusion of the planned Capital Return dividend would also increase the prospective 2027 yield to about 4.6%.

However, investors must recognise that this higher yield includes a time-limited payout.

At S$69.72 per share, DBS trades at around 2.85 times its net book value of S$24.47 per share as at 30 September 2026.

This multiple is known as the price-to-book (P/B) ratio.

The premium reflects DBS’s strong profitability, with return on equity reaching 17% for 9M2026.

However, its relatively high valuation also means that a slowdown in earnings growth could weigh on its share price.

Furthermore, investors should consider the risks of putting nearly all their S$10,000 into a single bank.

If investors spread their capital across different companies and sectors, it could help reduce their exposure to DBS’s performance.

Get Smart: How Much Can S$10,000 in DBS Really Earn?

Based on its current dividend payments and planned capital returns, having a S$10,000 investment in DBS could generate between S$420 and S$487 in dividend income in 2027.

The base case estimate of S$454 annually appears reasonable given DBS’s resilient earnings, capital position and current ordinary dividend level.

However, investors should note that the capital return dividend is only planned through 2027 and ordinary dividends are dependent on future profitability.

Ultimately, DBS is an appealing dividend stock, but its relatively high valuation means investors should weigh income received against potential capital losses.

A reliable dividend is valuable, but paying the right price for that income matters just as much.

data.title: Get Smart: Nvidia Has Fallen 35%. Should You Buy, Hold or Sell?
data.description:
Singapore investors have been buying Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) after its latest sell-off.

And it seems like they have been buying enthusiastically.

According to The Business Times, Nvidia orders on Syfe surged to around 13 times the daily average of the previous six weeks after Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive last Thursday. Seventy per cent of Syfe clients who traded US stocks that day were trading Nvidia.

I understand the temptation.

I own Nvidia shares too.

The stock has fallen roughly 35% from its record high in early October. A company you already liked is suddenly available at a much lower price.

Surely that makes it a buying opportunity?

Maybe.

But before I ask whether I should buy more Nvidia, I think there is a harder question worth answering first.

Should I still own it at all?

What changed besides the share price?

Buying the dip sounds sensible because we tend to assume that the company we liked before is now simply cheaper.

Sometimes, that is exactly what has happened.

But not every falling share price is a bargain.

If something has changed about the business itself, then investors need to reassess what the company is worth and how much risk they are taking.

And quite a lot has changed at Nvidia.

Jensen Huang did not just occupy the CEO’s office. He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it for 33 years.

He helped drive the launch of CUDA, pushed Nvidia towards artificial intelligence long before it became mainstream, managed some of its biggest customer relationships and represented the company in Washington on China export rules.

His sudden departure therefore creates genuine key-person risk.

Nvidia has appointed long-time CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

The question is not whether Nvidia can function without Jensen Huang. Of course it can.

The harder question is how much of the company’s extraordinary success came from decisions or actions that were uniquely his.

And it is likely that we won’t know the answer for some time.

The bigger risk may not be Jensen Huang

There is another issue that worries me more.

Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation following reports that Jensen Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence effort.

For investors, the important question is not the sensational part of the story.

It is whether the fallout ultimately affects Nvidia’s business.

In particular, could it result in tighter US controls over where Nvidia’s advanced chips can be sold?

That matters because China and export restrictions were already a major risk for the company before this happened.

If tighter rules apply broadly to American chipmakers, Nvidia could lose part of its addressable market.

But Nvidia-specific restrictions could be more damaging. Customers might then have more reason to move orders to competitors such as AMD.

In other words, this isn’t simply bad publicity.

There is a possible pathway from today’s headlines to Nvidia’s future revenue.

That deserves our attention.

But what hasn’t changed?

This is where things get more complicated.

Nvidia’s business did not suddenly stop growing when Jensen Huang resigned.

Its most recent quarter generated US$96.2 billion in revenue, more than double the amount a year earlier.

Its near-term product roadmap was also developed while Jensen Huang was still running the company, and many customer orders have already been placed.

Nvidia also benefits from its CUDA software platform, which developers use to build AI applications. Because so much AI software has been developed around Nvidia’s technology, switching to competing chips isn’t always straightforward.

Meanwhile, the world’s biggest technology companies are still spending heavily on AI infrastructure.

These are reasons why I don’t think the answer is automatically “sell”.

But I don’t think it is automatically “buy the dip” either.

Buy, hold or sell?

For existing Nvidia shareholders, I think there are three reasonable questions to ask.

Would I buy more?

Perhaps, if I believe Nvidia’s long-term competitive advantages remain intact and the lower share price more than compensates me for the additional uncertainty.

Would I hold?

That may make sense if my original investment thesis remains intact, but I want to see how the leadership transition and investigations develop before committing more money.

Would I sell or trim?

I would have to consider this if Jensen Huang himself was a major reason I invested or if the regulatory risks have moved beyond my comfort level.

Or perhaps Nvidia has grown into such a large position that I am carrying more risk than I intended.

There isn’t one answer for every investor.

But there is one question all of us should be asking.

Get Smart: A cheaper stock isn’t necessarily a better bargain

When shares fall, it is tempting to focus on how much cheaper they have become.

But price is only one half of the equation.

If the risks surrounding a company have increased at the same time, then a lower price may simply reflect a different investment proposition.

Some might believe that a 35% decline has handed them an opportunity to buy more.

Maybe it has.

But for me, I want to answer a more important question first: 

What has changed besides the price?

Net profit climbed 102.8% YoY to S$6.4 million, also a quarterly record, while gross margin widened to a 20-quarter high of 55.0%, from 51.5% a year ago.

The company links its outlook to wider industry demand, noting that global chip sales grew amid strong demand for AI, computing and memory, while it continues to see strong demand across its key markets.

Under a five-year strategy launched in FY2027, Micro-Mechanics aims to double revenue from FY2026 levels to at least S$150 million by FY2031.

Its balance sheet also stands out, with S$33.3 million in cash and no bank borrowings as at 30 September 2026.

Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure), however, slipped 10.6% YoY to S$3.7 million as capital expenditure rose to S$0.9 million from S$0.3 million.

Spending is set to climb further, with the company planning to invest S$12.0 million in FY2027 to expand its manufacturing footprint.

No dividend was declared for the quarter, in line with its practice of usually declaring dividends in the second and fourth quarters.

The company says its net cash position allows it to pay consistent dividends.

Can Digital Core REIT’s data centres grow its DPU?

Digital Core REIT is a data centre real estate investment trust (REIT) sponsored by Digital Realty.

As at 30 September 2026, before a pending portfolio transaction, it owned 11 freehold data centres across the US, Canada, Germany and Japan.

It holds assets under management of US$1.9 billion.

Demand for data centres is showing up in rental rates, with new and renewal leases signed in the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026) achieving a cash rental reversion of 23%.

Management cites growth in AI workloads as a demand driver, but this has yet to translate into stronger income.

For 9M2026, revenue rose 1.6% YoY to US$134.5 million, but net property income (NPI) fell 4.3% to US$64.8 million, mainly due to the redevelopment of 8217 Linton Hall Road in Northern Virginia.

Distributable income to unitholders also slipped 1.1% YoY to US$34.8 million.

There could be an improvement ahead, as Linton Hall is now fully leased.

The lease is expected to start on 1 December 2026 and add US$18.1 million in annualised rent.

Management expects 2027 DPU of between US$0.0415 and US$0.0425, compared with a trailing 12-month distribution of US$0.0360, implying growth of roughly 15% to 18%.

Risks remain, though: in-service occupancy stood at 97.0%, while Los Angeles occupancy slipped to 84.1% from 85.6% as at 30 June 2026.

The pending portfolio transaction, which includes buying a 2.5% stake in a Singapore data centre, would also see the REIT enter Singapore.

The transaction would reduce aggregate leverage from 41.6% to 37.6% on a pro forma basis.

Where does Info-Tech Systems fit into the AI story?

Info-Tech Systems is a software-as-a-service (SaaS) provider of cloud-based HR, accounting and customer relationship management (CRM) software, serving more than 28,000 businesses across five countries.

Its AI connection is through people rather than infrastructure, as its Info-Tech Academy runs AI-related training courses that have helped drive growth in its services business.

For 9M2026, revenue rose 20% YoY to S$42.6 million, while subscription revenue, which accounts for about three-quarters of the total, grew 11% to S$32.2 million.

Services revenue grew much faster, rising 82% YoY to S$8.6 million on demand for the Academy’s AI-related WSQ courses in Singapore.

Services now account for 20% of revenue, up from 13% a year ago.

Dividend investors, however, have less information to work with, as the update relied on unaudited management accounts and did not disclose profit or free cash flow.

Its CEO described a strong cash position and a debt-free balance sheet but gave no figures, and the update made no mention of dividends.

Management expects demand for Academy courses to normalise after an exceptional surge in 4Q2025, which came ahead of the expiry of a S$500 SkillsFuture Credit top-up.

This leaves a high base for the fourth quarter.

Get Smart: Buy the dividend, not the theme

All three companies point to AI as a source of demand, but that does not automatically make them good income investments.

Dividend investors need to look beyond the theme and check whether each business generates enough cash after funding its growth.

Does it have a track record of returning that cash to shareholders?

On the figures disclosed, Micro-Mechanics clears both checks. 

Digital Core REIT is counting on a lease expected to start in December.

Info-Tech has yet to disclose enough information to assess its cash generation and dividend prospects.

Before buying any AI-linked stock for income, ask yourself one question: when the excitement fades, will this business still pay you?

data.description:
When companies buy back their own shares, they are putting their own cash behind their stock. 

Over the five sessions to 5 November 2026, three dividend-paying stocks on the Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) did just that.

Data from Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68), or SGX, shows that 19 primary-listed companies bought back shares over the period, spending a combined S$11.1 million. 

United Overseas Bank Ltd (SGX: U11), or UOB, and Seatrium Limited (SGX: 5E2) accounted for the two biggest purchases, spending S$4.59 million between them, or about 41.5% of the total.

SGX took a different approach.

How much did each company spend on buybacks?

Company Shares Repurchased Total Buyback Value Average Price Paid
United Overseas Bank 68,000 S$2,590,368 S$38.09
Seatrium 1,085,000 S$1,997,653 S$1.84
Singapore Exchange 6,000 S$120,999 S$20.17
Three Combined 1,159,000 S$4,709,020 –

Note: Figures cover market purchases from 30 October to 5 November 2026, and buyback value includes stamp duties and clearing charges.

Why is UOB the week’s biggest buyer?

UOB topped the table, with its buyback accounting for 23.4% of the week’s total buyback value.

Its results for the quarter ended 30 September 2026 (3Q2026) provide useful context, with net fee income rising 19% year on year (YoY) to a record S$733 million on growth in wealth, cards and loan-related activities.

Gross customer loans also grew 6.0% YoY to S$372.3 billion.

Margins, however, moved in the opposite direction as the net interest margin narrowed to 1.68%, from 1.82% a year ago, mainly due to higher deposit costs.

Net profit attributable to shareholders came in at S$1.3 billion, up 182.2% YoY, although this increase came off a low base after UOB set aside S$1.4 billion in allowances, including pre-emptive provisions, a year earlier.

UOB did not declare a dividend alongside its 3Q2026 results, in line with its practice of paying dividends twice a year.

For 2027, the bank expects mid-single-digit loan growth and total credit costs of 25 to 30 basis points.

What sits behind Seatrium’s buyback?

Seatrium bought the most shares of the three companies, while its buyback value ranked second for the week.

For the first half ended 30 June 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 4.7% YoY to S$5.6 billion, with ship and rig building or conversion revenue climbing 17.5% to S$4.2 billion and more than offsetting a 29% decline in offshore platforms revenue.

Profit attributable to owners rose 158.3% YoY to S$372.9 million, but this figure includes a one-off S$171.7 million gain on the disposal of non-core assets.

Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure) was negative S$11.6 million, an improvement from negative S$31.9 million a year earlier.

Seatrium recognised revenue ahead of billings, lifting contract assets by S$1.6 billion to S$6.5 billion, while its balance sheet showed S$1.7 billion in cash against S$2.4 billion of debt, excluding lease liabilities, as at 30 June 2026.

Seatrium pays dividends once a year, so it declared no interim dividend for 1H2026.

Management guided that FY2026 net profit should come in materially higher than FY2025, helped by the one-off divestment gains.

How does SGX reward shareholders instead?

SGX ranked 15th out of the 19 companies by buyback value, with dividends doing most of the work for its shareholders.

For the financial year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), net revenue grew 13.9% YoY to S$1.5 billion, while net profit rose 7.8% to S$698.4 million after a S$53.4 million goodwill impairment on its indices business.

Excluding that impairment and other adjustments, adjusted net profit rose 24.6% to S$759.5 million.

Free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capital expenditure) grew 2.0% to S$788.8 million.

SGX held S$1.8 billion in cash against S$628.2 million in borrowings, giving it a net cash position of about S$1.18 billion.

Its FY2026 dividends comprised:

  • Ordinary dividends: S$0.445 per share
  • One-off additional dividend: S$0.125 per share
  • Total: S$0.570 per share, up from S$0.375 a year earlier

Management guided for quarterly dividend increases of S$0.0025 per share through FY2028 and full repayment of debt in FY2027.

Get Smart: Follow the cash behind the buyback

A buyback shows that a company is willing to spend, but it does not tell you whether that spending can be repeated.

Before treating a buyback as a vote of confidence, look at where the money comes from and whether recurring profit and cash flow can support both dividends and share repurchases.

It is also worth stripping out one-off gains before judging the profit line, as Seatrium’s disposal gain illustrates.

For a bank like UOB, keep an eye on net profit and credit costs, while for SGX and Seatrium, free cash flow deserves closer attention because it is the lifeblood of dividends.

data.title: Is the Great Singapore REIT Comeback Finally Here?
data.description:
Singapore real estate investment trusts (REITs) have had a frustrating couple of years. 

The iEdge S-REIT Index (SGX: SRU) was down about 14.1% year to date as at 13 November 2026 against the Straits Times Index’s (SGX: ^STI) 12.3% gain. 

Yet, some REITs are quietly growing their distributions again. 

So, is this the start of a proper recovery or just a pause before the next leg down? 

The answer depends on more than interest rates. 

Why Singapore REITs Have Struggled and What’s Different Now 

Higher interest rates did most of the damage. 

When rates went up, REITs had to refinance their loans at higher costs, leaving less to pay out as distributions per unit (DPU). 

Meanwhile, income investors could earn a decent return from T-bills and fixed deposits without taking any risk. 

Some REITs also struggled with falling property values or weak overseas performance, while banks and growth stocks pulled money away. 

Some of that pressure is lifting. 

Local interest rates have eased, so older loans are being refinanced more cheaply. 

Singapore offices and malls are signing leases at higher rents, occupancy rates are still firm, and many REITs still trade below their net asset value (NAV). 

If these trends hold, the three REITs below could benefit. 

How the Three REITs Compare

REIT Yield DPU Trend Gearing Rental Reversion Recovery Catalyst
Suntec REIT (SGX: T82U) 6.0% Increasing 43.0% Overall Positive Divestment of Australian assets
NTT DC REIT (SGX: NTDU) 5.9%* Maiden DPU 31.0% Overall Positive Rental growth, acquisitions
Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust (SGX: SET) 9.0% Increasing 43.6% Overall Positive Office segment to stabilise

*Note: Not annualised; 261-day period.

Suntec looks the most defensive, NTT DC REIT has the clearest growth, and SET offers the highest yield for those willing to take on more risk. 

Suntec REIT (SGX: T82U) – Strong Rents That Benefit From Lower Rates

Suntec REIT is best known for Suntec City, and it also owns stakes in One Raffles Quay and Marina Bay Financial Centre. 

Outside Singapore, it has offices in Australia and the UK.  

Business at home is going well. 

As at 30 September 2026 (3Q2026), its Singapore offices were 99.6% occupied and its malls 98.6%. 

In 3Q2026, rental reversions were 7.3% for its Singapore offices and 11.2% for its malls. 


DPU for the first nine months (9M2026) rose 20.7% year on year (YoY), helped by lower interest costs. 

At a unit price of S$1.35 as at 13 November 2026, Suntec REIT offers a trailing distribution yield of 6.0% and trades at about 0.66x its net asset value (NAV) of S$2.04 per unit. 

The main weakness is debt. 

Gearing climbed to 43.0%, and an interest coverage ratio (ICR) of 2.3x. 

Its all-in financing cost has fallen to 3.57%, from 3.71% at 31 December 2025. 

Should Suntec manage to sell its three Australian assets, gearing could improve from current levels. 

Management expects future DPU growth to be from higher Singapore rents and lower financing costs. 

The main risks for Suntec would likely be from its overseas holdings and higher financing costs. 

NTT DC REIT (SGX: NTDU) – The Growth Recovery Play

This data centre REIT owns six properties in the US, Austria, and Singapore. 

That’s a rare corner of property where rents are still climbing at a healthy clip. 

Its maiden DPU, ending 31 March 2026 (FY2025/2026), came in at US$0.0556.

At a unit price of US$0.945 as at 13 November 2026, this works out to an estimated distribution yield of 5.9%. 

Do note this distribution covered less than a full year. 

For the first quarter ended 30 June 2026 (1QFY2026/2027), portfolio occupancy was 95.9% (rising to 99.2% once signed leases start), and renewals were signed at rents 13.4% higher. 

The balance sheet leaves plenty of room for acquisition-fuelled growth.

Gearing is at 31%, while its ICR stands at 4.7x. 

No loans fall due for two years, and the REIT has US$261 million of debt headroom before it reaches its 40% gearing limit. 

The main risks include rising power costs, 14% of rent that’s up for renewal in this financial year, and a concentrated tenant base where the top 10 pay 74.5% of rent. 

Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust (SGX: SET) – The High-Yield Opportunity

Stoneweg Europe, or SERT, owns mostly logistics and office properties across Europe. 

At a unit price of €1.50 as at 13 November 2026, it yields about 9.0% and trades at roughly 0.74x NAV.

The distribution looks steady for now. 

Distribution per stapled security (DPS) rose 1.4% to €0.0664 in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026).

As at its 3Q2026 business update on 12 November 2026, management upgraded its FY2026 DPS guidance to be at least €0.1339. 

Logistics / light industrial rent reversion was 8.6%, with an occupancy rate of 94.9%, so why are the units trading near 52-week lows? 

Offices are the drag. 

SERT’s office occupancy was only 90.5%, and rent reversion was 1.9%.

Gearing looks manageable at 42.9%, with an ICR of 2.9x. 

Crucially, 89% of its debt is hedged, and there’s no major refinancing until 2030. 

This gives the REIT some time before its office segment recovers. 

SERT is also moving into data centres, which could provide some potential upside, but this brings execution risk. 

On balance, the yield is tempting, but you’re being paid to accept weaker office performance and a big strategy shift (into data centres). 

What Could Stop the REIT Comeback?

Another Fed rate hike, or rates that stay elevated, would keep refinancing costs up. 

Weaker rents, further declines in property values or fresh DPU cuts would also hurt. 

Finally, the continued preference for banks, risk-free income alternatives, or growth stocks could keep investors away from REITs. 

Cheap REITs can stay cheap if the reasons behind the discount don’t change. 

Get Smart: A Recovery Worth Watching

S-REITs could be close to a turning point, though a lot still depends on where interest rates go. 

And even if sentiment picks up, some REITs will recover much faster than others.

The ones to look for have growing rents and debt that’s under control, because those are the REITs most able to raise DPU. 

Investors who focus on these qualities may be well placed if the sector’s recovery takes hold.

data.description:
Singaporean investors love a good dividend.

This earnings season, the bigger story sat one line above the payout.

Two Singapore-listed financial companies set records in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q2026).

United Overseas Bank Limited (SGX: U11), or UOB, earned a record S$733 million in net fees.

iFAST Corporation Ltd (SGX: AIY) ended the quarter with a record S$36.8 billion in assets under administration (AUA).

Here’s the thing: both records arrived while bank lending margins shrank.

UOB’s net interest margin (NIM) narrowed to 1.68% from 1.82% a year ago. 

At DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), NIM fell to 1.87% from 1.96%.

Why should you care?

Banks earn fees on the money they manage and the services they sell, so fee income ties up less capital than lending. 

Fee income also depends less on interest rates.

So which of these three companies turns fee growth into dividends most directly? 

Let’s start with the smallest.

Net interest margin Not applicable 1.87% (from 1.96%) 1.68% (from 1.82%)
Dividend declared S$0.0320, up 39.1% S$0.66 ordinary and S$0.15 capital return None (pays half-yearly)

How much of iFAST’s growth keeps coming back?

iFAST runs a global digital banking and wealth management platform.

It serves retail investors through FSM Global, and financial advisers and institutions through its business-to-business arm.

Its AUA rose 20.0% year on year (YoY) to a record S$36.8 billion.

Clients added S$1.24 billion of net inflows, and rising markets helped too.

Better still, most of iFAST’s income repeats.

Recurring net revenue grew 22.0% YoY to S$95.4 million, which made up 86.2% of net revenue.

Net profit attributable to owners rose 24.5% YoY to S$32.4 million.

And shareholders are getting a bigger slice.

The third interim dividend rose 39.1% YoY to S$0.0320.

Management expects a FY2026 dividend of at least S$0.1200, above its April 2026 guidance of S$0.1050.

On the flip side, iFAST now carries more debt.

Borrowings, excluding lease liabilities, rose to S$234.3 million from S$113.1 million at the end of 2025. 

A S$120 million note issue in March 2026 accounts for most of the increase.

Can DBS’s fees make up for a weak trading quarter?

DBS serves retail, wealth and corporate customers across Asia.

Its customer businesses kept growing.

Net fee and commission income rose 6% YoY to S$1.43 billion, and treasury customer sales and other income grew 19% to S$685 million.

Trading was a different story.

Markets trading non-interest income fell to S$17 million from S$419 million a year ago.

Net profit for the quarter dropped 4.8% to S$2.81 billion.

To be sure, one weak quarter doesn’t undo the year. 

Net profit for the first nine months of 2026 reached a record S$8.82 billion.

The dividend comes in two parts, so read them separately.

DBS declared an ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share and a capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share.

The S$0.81 total is 8% higher than the S$0.75 paid a year ago.

Management expects structural growth in wealth management to continue. 

For 2027, it guides for total income growth in the mid-single-digit range.

Is UOB’s record fee haul enough to lift its payout?

UOB serves more than 8 million customers across the region.

Its net fee income rose 19% YoY to the record S$733 million, with wealth, cards and loan-related activities driving the gain.

The rest of the bank had a tougher quarter.

Other non-interest income fell 29% to S$370 million on lower trading and investment income.

Operating profit before allowances declined 2.8% to S$1.8 billion, while total expenses rose 2%.

If you’re waiting for a dividend, it’s not due yet.

UOB pays dividends twice a year, so it declared none this quarter. 

That’s a matter of timing, not a cut.

Look closer at the 2027 guidance.

UOB expects fee income to grow at a mid- to high-single-digit pace and operating costs to rise at a similar rate.

If both forecasts hold, fees alone won’t widen the gap between income and costs.

UOB says it is investing in capital-light businesses that broaden its sources of revenue.

Get Smart: Follow the fees, then follow the payout

A record fee number is a good start.

But it doesn’t tell you how much of that money reaches you.

When the next set of results arrives, check whether the fee line is growing faster than costs.

Then check whether the dividend follows.

iFAST’s recurring revenue and its dividend are both rising today.

DBS has raised its total payout.

As for UOB, the answer comes with its final dividend for 2026.

Keep asking both questions, quarter after quarter.

data.title: Jensen Huang Resigns: What NVIDIA’s CEO Exit Teaches You About Key-Man Risk
data.description:
NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) lost a key co-founder last week.

Jensen Huang built the chipmaker over 33 years. 

On 12 November 2026, he resigned as chief executive officer with immediate effect. 

He also left the board. 

There are no prizes for guessing why. 

But what about investors? 

A line often attributed to Warren Buffett fits the moment. 

“I try to invest in businesses that are so wonderful that an idiot can run them. Because sooner or later, one will.”

Let me be clear: Jensen Huang is no idiot. 

He has, however, left some big shoes to fill. 

A great company should keep its edge after its founder walks out the door.

What happens at NVIDIA now?

Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s chief financial officer, is now interim CEO. 

She will be at the helm until the board names a permanent successor. 

Harvey C. Jones, a former chief executive of chip-design software firm Synopsys (NASDAQ: SNPS), becomes the board’s first-ever chair.

The board will consider internal and external candidates, and it has not set a timeline. 

As you can tell, there are many open questions.

You can expect analysts to have a field day when NVIDIA reports its third-quarter results on 17 November 2026, as scheduled.

Jones said the company expects its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap “to continue without interruption”.

Why does one departure matter so much?

Huang ran NVIDIA unlike most chief executives. 

He had about 60 direct reports, and he skipped one-on-one meetings in favour of group sessions.

That set-up let decisions move fast. 

It also meant much of NVIDIA’s judgement rested on one person.

In the near term, demand for AI chips may carry the business. 

The harder test comes later, when NVIDIA’s next leader has to pick the company’s big long-term bets without him.

How can you spot key-man risk in your own portfolio?

NVIDIA is listed in the US, but SGX companies can carry the same risk. 

You can check for it in your own holdings.

Look at who chairs the board. An independent chair who is not the CEO gives the board a voice of its own. NVIDIA named its first chair in the same announcement as Huang’s exit.

Read the management pages of the annual report. A deep bench of senior executives with long tenures gives the board people it can promote from within.

Search for succession planning. The corporate governance report should explain how the nominating committee plans for a change of CEO. A vague answer or missing statement is a signal too.

Ask where the advantage sits. An edge built on assets, contracts, or customer relationships lasts longer than one built on a single person’s judgement.

Get Smart: Own the business, not the boss

A great leader is a good reason to like a stock. 

It should not be your only reason.

Before you buy, ask yourself this: if the CEO resigned tomorrow, would you still want to own the shares? 

If your answer is no, your investment case rests on one person. 

Size your position with that in mind.

data.title: How to Balance REIT Dividends with US Growth Stocks for Maximum Returns
data.description:
Ask the people around you how they want to grow their wealth, and the answer is usually one of two things: steady dividends or capital appreciation.

And the go-to is usually Singapore real estate investment trusts (S-REITs) for the former and US tech giants for the latter. 

However, going all-in on either means taking on all of its weak spots.

When you mix REITs with US growth stocks, you strike a balance between consistent cash flow and long-term upside. 

Here’s how to make them work together.

Why Combine REITs and US Growth Stocks?

REITs own income-generating properties like malls and warehouses, collect rent, and pay out 90%+ of taxable income for corporate tax breaks. 

That high payout makes them an income favourite. 

Reinvest the payout, and watch your money snowball faster. 

On the flip side, big tech stalwarts like Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ: GOOGL), and Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ: AMZN) skip the hefty payouts and pour their cash directly into expansion, especially AI and cloud infrastructure. 

They run on entirely different engines.

Blending them gives you sensible diversification, but don’t treat it like a bulletproof hedge. 

When a sharp sell-off strikes, both can easily drop at the same time. 

Choosing the Right Singapore REITs for Dividend Income

A fat yield means little if the payout behind it is shrinking. 

So before buying a REIT, always check if its payout is growing. 

CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), Singapore’s largest REIT, raised its distribution per unit (DPU) by 7.1% to S$0.0602 in 1H2026. 

This was driven by strong rental reversions of 4.0% in retail and 6.5% in offices, alongside a resilient occupancy rate of 95.6%.

In contrast, Mapletree Industrial Trust (SGX: ME8U)’s 1HFY2026/2027 DPU slipped 5.7% to S$0.0608 after property sales and weaker occupancy at its North American portfolio. 

A headline yield above 6% is definitely juicy, but a declining payout quickly erodes that initial appeal. 

Balance sheet strength also plays a critical role.

When interest rates stay elevated, a REIT’s gearing directly impacts the bottom line. 

CICT maintains a gearing ratio of 37.4% with an average cost of debt at 2.9%.

Healthcare pure-play Parkway Life REIT (SGX: C2PU) runs even leaner at 33.8% gearing, helping power a 14.6% jump in its 1H2026 DPU on the back of rising Singapore hospital rents.

That’s why sector diversification matters too!

Malls, offices, hospitals, and warehouses all answer to different tenants, so a slump in one won’t sink your payouts. 

Selecting US Growth Stocks for Long-Term Capital Appreciation

For a growth company to stay great, it needs something special, something rivals find hard to copy.

Companies like Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon have that kind of edge. 

Microsoft reported 19.0% year-on-year (YoY) growth in revenue to US$92.3 billion for 1QFY2027, with its Azure cloud business up 48.0%. 

Alphabet’s 3Q2026 revenue climbed 25.0% YoY to US$127.6 billion as Google Cloud revenue soared 103.0%. 

Similarly, Amazon posted 12.0% YoY growth to US$201.9 billion for 3Q2026, as AWS sales were up 39.0%. 

However, growth only counts if it eventually becomes free cash flow. 

And here’s where the picture splits. 

Over the past 12 months, Microsoft generated US$60.0 billion of free cash flow and Alphabet US$19.4 billion, although Alphabet’s quarterly free cash flow has dipped below zero in each of the last two quarters. 

Meanwhile, Amazon swung to a negative US$42.4 billion as its AI spending ballooned. 

That said, negative cash flow is not necessarily bad if those data centres pay off, but it is still a risk to watch. 

How Much Should You Allocate to REITs vs US Growth Stocks?

There’s no perfect asset split for everyone.

It simply comes down to your age, goals, and how many ups and downs you can stomach.

If you’re close to retiring, locking in consistent cash flow and capital preservation takes priority.  

But if you have decades ahead, you can ride out bigger swings for more growth.

Here is a hypothetical S$100,000 split. 

Portfolio Style S-REITs US Growth Stocks Rough Yearly Payout Suits
Income-focused 70% 30% S$3,920 Near or in retirement
Balanced 50% 50% S$2,900 Mid-career
Growth-focused 30% 70% S$1,880 Young, long horizon

Assumes average distribution yields of 5.45% for S-REIT and dividend yields of 0.35% for US growth stocks.

The income-focused mix pays the most today and swings the least, but grows more slowly.

The growth-focused mix pays little now but has the most upside, and bumpiest ride. 

Remember, this two-asset combo is just a baseline model, not a complete portfolio. 

You’ll still want an emergency cash cushion, some bond allocation for ballast, and broad-market shares outside of property and tech.

How Dividends and Growth Can Work Together

While you are building wealth, reinvest your REIT distributions into more units, or into growth stocks when their valuations look reasonable. 

That helps rebalance your portfolio without selling anything. 

As retirement nears, gradually shift towards income. 

Let your stage of life drive the change and not the latest headlines. 

What Are the Risks of Combining REITs and US Growth Stocks?

Interest rates are one of the most important risks to watch, as they cut both ways. 

Higher rates raise REIT borrowing costs and tend to drag down growth-stock prices too. 

Currency is another. 

As US stocks are priced in US dollars, if the greenback weakens against the Singapore dollar, your returns shrink when converted back. 

Also, watch out for concentration.

Having three technology giants or five shopping malls is not diversification. 

Lastly, volatility. 

Both can drop 20% or more, so keep an emergency fund and you’ll never be forced to sell at the bottom. 

How to Measure Whether Your Portfolio Is Working

Watch your total return – payouts plus price changes. 

A 7% yielder whose unit price falls 10% has still lost you money. 

Check that your REITs’ DPU rises over time and review your portfolio at least once a year. 

If your mix drifts off target, rebalance based on business fundamentals, not price swings. 

Get Smart: Balance Income Today with Growth Tomorrow

REITs pay you now while growth stocks build wealth for later. 

Whatever the mix, judge each holding on payout quality, debt, and cash flow, not just its yield. 

That goal is never to buy the biggest yield or hottest stock. 

It’s simply to build a portfolio that delivers solid total returns and fits your life.

data.description:
Welcome to this week’s edition of top stock market highlights.

A chipmaker that was the world’s most valuable company just weeks ago lost its long-time leader this week, and its shares tumbled.

Closer to home, market volatility lifted the local bourse’s derivatives trading volume to a six-month high in October.

Meanwhile, US bond yields climbed back above 5% as investors braced for more interest rate hikes.

And in a bright spot for Singapore, a global pension index ranked the country’s retirement system the best in Asia.

Nvidia’s CEO resigns as scandal deepens

Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA) announced on 12 November 2026 that co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned following reports of two affairs.

Scrutiny began after Huang admitted to a relationship with a former executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed International. 

US authorities suspect her of spying for China, a claim Beijing has denied. 

A later report said Huang had also had a relationship with a senior Nvidia executive who reported to him.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent successor. 

Board member Harvey Jones has been appointed Nvidia’s first-ever chair. 

Huang, who owns about 3.6% of the company, will also leave the board.

The shares fell as much as 14% at the open, pushing Nvidia’s market capitalisation below US$4 trillion for the first time since 2025. 

The stock is now roughly 35% below its early-October record, and at least seven Wall Street firms have downgraded it over the past week.

Investors will look to Nvidia’s 3QFY2027 results, due on 17 November 2026, for clarity.

Market volatility lifts SGX’s trading volumes

Singapore Exchange (SGX: S68) reported on 12 November 2026 that its derivatives daily average volume climbed to a six-month high in October, as volatile markets drove demand for hedging.

Daily average derivatives volume rose 8% year on year and 17% month on month to 1.6 million contracts. FTSE China A50 Index Futures recorded a 24-month high in daily average volume. 

Open interest (the value of contracts still outstanding) in GIFT Nifty 50 contracts topped US$20 billion.

Securities market turnover also rose, climbing 32% year on year to S$44.8 billion. 

Daily average value reached S$2 billion, driven by trading in index stocks and REITs.

The pick-up came as Singapore shares weakened in October. 

The Straits Times Index (SGX: ^STI) fell about 5% to 5,376.74, while the FTSE ST Technology Index dropped 17%.

Even so, the STI ended the month 21% higher than a year earlier.

US bond yields climb as bets on rate hikes grow

US Treasury yields rose sharply on 12 November 2026, with the benchmark 10-year yield climbing back above 5% to 5.068%. 

The two-year yield, which is more sensitive to Federal Reserve policy, jumped more than 11 basis points (0.11 percentage point) to 4.843%.

Hotter-than-expected consumer price index (CPI) data earlier in the week strengthened expectations of further rate hikes. 

Traders are now fully pricing in a hike in December, and Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) added another quarter-point hike in March 2027 to its forecast.

Oil added to inflation worries after President Donald Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran. 

That raised concerns the war in the Middle East could drag on, and Brent crude rose about 1% to US$93.60 a barrel.

Higher rates are already weighing on rate-sensitive sectors. 

US existing home sales fell to their lowest level in more than 16 years in October.

For Singapore investors, rising rates could mean higher borrowing costs for REITs. 

The impact on local banks is more mixed, as the 3Q2026 results for DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation Limited (SGX: O39) and United Overseas Bank Limited (SGX: U11) showed.

Singapore’s retirement system ranks first in Asia

Singapore’s retirement system ranked fourth in the world and first in Asia in the Marsh CFA Institute Global Pension Index 2026, released on 20 October 2026.

Singapore scored 82.0 out of 100, earning an A grade alongside just five other systems. 

The Netherlands topped the index with 85.8, followed by Denmark (84.1) and Iceland (84.0). Israel and Australia completed the A-grade group.

The index assessed 55 retirement income systems on three measures:

  • Adequacy (40% weighting)
  • Sustainability (35%)
  • Integrity (25%)

It measures the overall strength of each system rather than comparing individual pension payouts.

Singapore finished well ahead of its regional peers. 

Hong Kong ranked 17th, Malaysia 35th and Japan 39th, while Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines were all in the bottom 10. 

The US placed 33rd.

A strong national system does not guarantee every individual a comfortable retirement, however. Depending on their goals, investors may still need their own savings and investments.

data.title: Should You Invest Your Child’s Money in DBS, an ETF or a REIT?
data.description:
Many parents tend to save the money their child receives from red packets into savings accounts for their future. 

While it is safe to keep it as cash, these savings can accumulate into a meaningful sum over time with the right investments.

The harder question is choosing where to invest it: In DBS Group Holdings Ltd (SGX: D05), a broad-market exchange-traded fund (ETF), or a quality Singapore real estate investment trust (S-REIT)?

A Snapshot: DBS vs ETF vs REIT

DBS ETF REIT
Diversification Low High Moderate
Income Dividends Depends on ETF Distributions
Growth potential Business-dependent Market-driven Property and rental growth
Key risk Single company/banking exposure Broad market declines Rates, debt and property cycles
Effort required Higher Lower Higher
Learning opportunity Business ownership Diversification Passive income/property

Option #1: DBS 

As Singapore’s largest bank, DBS is a familiar blue-chip business with an established track record of both profitability and shareholder returns. 

That record has held up even as interest rates fell. 

DBS’s total income for the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026) rose 2% year on year (YoY) to a new high of S$17.9 billion, and net profit climbed 2% YoY to a record S$8.82 billion.

Total income for 3Q2026 slipped 1% YoY to S$5.85 billion and net profit fell 5% YoY to S$2.81 billion, mainly because of lower markets trading income. 

Net interest income, the bank’s core lending earnings, still grew 4% YoY to S$3.71 billion.

The bank declared a 3Q2026 ordinary dividend of S$0.66 per share, plus a capital return dividend of S$0.15 per share.

Reinvesting the dividend can buy more shares, generating more payouts for your child in the future. 

With DBS, parents can also easily introduce the idea of owning part of a real business to their child.

However, putting a large portion of your child’s money into a single stock, even one as strong as DBS Group, can be risky.

If anything happens to the bank or the banking sector in general, the investment could fall sharply in value. 

Option #2: A Broad-Market ETF

With a broad-market exchange-traded fund (ETF), your child’s money enjoys diversification from the very first dollar. 

For example, Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA: VOO) tracks 500 large-cap U.S. companies, offering access to technology and scalable global sectors absent from the Singapore market. 

With one investment, the money gains exposure to 500 companies, without parents analysing and attempting to pick the biggest winner.

With a broad-market ETF, poor performance from an individual company has less impact on the overall portfolio. 

That said, returns will broadly follow the underlying market. 

As at 31 October 2026, the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF has returned 11.76% year-to-date and an average 12.04% a year over the past five years.

In comparison, the share price of Apple Inc (NASDAQ: AAPL), maker of the iPhone, rose by an average of about 18.1% a year over the same five years, and it is up around 26.8% so far in 2026.

By owning the whole market, investors give up the chance to significantly outperform it through a single standout stock.

When investing in ETFs, Singapore investors need to consider ETFs’ expense ratios, management fees, and any foreign exchange risk.

Option #3: A Singapore REIT

S-REITs turn your child’s savings into property income, without buying physical real estate. 

A favourite amongst Singapore investors, S-REITs typically pay out at least 90% of their taxable income to enjoy tax transparency.

Defensive REITs like CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust (SGX: C38U), or CICT, generate steady cash flows through regular distributions, which can be reinvested to accelerate growth.

However, a REIT’s income is highly dependent on factors like occupancy levels, rental growth, and interest rates.

Gearing, interest costs and debt maturities can affect the distribution per unit (DPU) and its sustainability. 

You might be in for a shock if you focus solely on headline yield without analysing the underlying business. 

Why Time Changes the Answer

A five-year-old gives you a powerful 15- to 20-year runway for compounding growth.

Short-term market volatility matters less when the investment has decades to grow.

And with the long investment horizon, compounding becomes the true force. 

Imagine you invest S$10,000 for your child, reinvesting the dividends and keeping the investment over the next decade or two:

10 years 15 years 20 years
3% returns S$13,439.16 S$15,579.67 S$18,061.11
4% returns S$14,802.44 S$18,009.44 S$21,911.23
5% returns S$16,288.95 S$20,789.28 S$26,532.98
6% returns S$17,908.48 S$23,965.58 S$32,071.35

Your S$10,000 more than tripled in 20 years with a 6% annual return, with dividends reinvested.

And then, there is capital appreciation.

Take DBS as an example.

On 16 October 2006, DBS shares traded at S$19.00 

By 12 November 2026, they had closed at S$71, nearly four times the earlier price. 

That’s a gain of about 274% before counting dividends or the bonus shares DBS has since issued to shareholders.

Do You Actually Have to Pick Just One?

Instead of an either-or choice, you can easily combine all three to minimise concentration risk while giving your child’s portfolio a chance to outperform the market. 

With an initial investment of S$10,000, you can split it into:

  • S$5,000: A broad-market ETF as a diversified core
  • S$2,500: DBS Group for capital appreciation and dividends
  • S$2,500: CICT for distributions and property exposure

Instead of 20 different stocks, keep it simple for your child’s portfolio. 

This makes it easier to teach them what they own and why these investments are chosen. 

The Most Important Investment May Not Be the Stock

Rather than focusing only on which stock is making money, show your child how you chose each investment, which companies they indirectly own and how payouts arrive. 

Through this, you teach them ownership, not speculation. 

This portfolio becomes an important financial education tool.

Your child can understand how underlying businesses earn, rather than focusing on daily share-price movements. 

By the time they take over the portfolio, they will have a better understanding of investing and will not be going into the market blind.   

Get Smart: Give Your Child Time and Ownership

DBS, ETFs, and REITs each offer something different.

A combination of all three can provide growth, income, and diversification.

Choosing that one winner today should not be a parent’s main aim, especially as a child has a long investment horizon that allows their investments to compound. 

The ultimate aim is not simply handing over the money to their child when they grow up but to offer an early understanding of how investment works and how to use it to build long-term wealth.
